claims.claim: Mordicai Knode says Wolfe does not lay out a trail of breadcrumbs in Peace but the clues are there.
claims.quote: doesn’t lay out breadcrumbs in a trail…but the clues are there
claims.page: body, section on the second layer

claims.claim: Mordicai Knode says the reader who chases all the details of Peace to their roots reaches the conclusion that the narrator is dead.
claims.quote: if you chase all the details to their roots
claims.page: body, section on the third layer

claims.claim: Mordicai Knode says the evidence that the narrator of Peace is dead is buried in the text but convincing.
claims.quote: The evidence for it is buried, but convincing.
claims.page: body, section on the third layer

claims.claim: Wowra says folk etymology is the primary method by which the narrator Latro records the place names in Soldier of the Mist.
claims.quote: it is the primary method Latro uses to record his place names

claims.claim: Wowra, classifying Latro's place names by George Stewart's toponymic taxonomy, says the predominant category is folk etymology, followed by descriptive, associative and commemorative names.
claims.quote: The predominant category is folk etymology, followed by the less frequent

claims.claim: Wowra says Latro records place names that do not match the sounds he heard because he is trying to communicate a deeper meaning about a place.
claims.quote: he is trying to communicate a deeper meaning about a place

claims.claim: Wolfe, in a Spring 1988 Weird Tales interview with Darrell Schweitzer reproduced by Wowra, says Latro calls Athens “Thought” because that is what he thinks it means, though his derivation is incorrect.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Darrell Schweitzer, Weird Tales, Spring 1988, quoted by Scott Wowra
claims.quote: Latro calls Athens Thought because that’s what he thinks it means.

claims.claim: Wowra quotes the Foreword of Soldier of the Mist saying the original writer sometimes wrote place names as he heard them and more often translated them when he believed he understood their meanings.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, Foreword to Soldier of the Mist (Tor hardback, 1986), quoted by Scott Wowra
claims.quote: I have followed the original writer, who sometimes wrote them as

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi and Nigel Price agree that Severian's post-historic vantage point means that all time in the Solar Cycle is vague.
claims.quote: Severian’s post-historic vantage point means that all time is vague

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi says Wolfe goes against the Vancean grain of numbered Aeons, contrasting Wolfe's vague reckoning with the numbered Aeons of Vance's Rhialto the Marvellous.
claims.quote: Wolfe goes against the Vancean grain of numbered Aeons

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi revises his own estimate of the span from Ymar to Severian to a range between one thousand and thirty-thousand years, most accurately “many chiliads”.
claims.quote: the range is actually between one thousand and thirty-thousand years

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi names as an elusive mystery the fact that the Autarch's name is never written in Severian's narrative.
claims.source: Michael Andre-Driussi, Ultan's Library, 27 August 2008 (essay written 1992)
claims.quote: why the Autarch’s name is never written in Severian’s narrative
claims.page: body, before the section on minor mysteries

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi says a character is described as being like a bear 22 chapters before the reader is given his name or his sobriquet.
claims.quote: 22 chapters before we are given his name or his sobriquet

claims.claim: Borski says the titular novella of The Fifth Head of Cerberus begins with a Proustian echo.
claims.quote: So begins, with its Proustian echo, the titular novella

claims.claim: Borski says the last sentence of the titular novella is as chilling as any written in science fiction and encapsulates the mindset of incipient tyrants.
claims.quote: the last sentence of the novella is as chilling as any
claims.page: review, paragraph on the first novella
